variants.name: Zero-sized marker types + PhantomData (consuming transitions)
variants.idiom_name: zero-sized marker types + PhantomData<S> + consuming transitions
variants.implementation_notes: The classic per-state class hierarchy collapses into one generic struct parameterized by a zero-sized marker type (struct Draft; struct Published;), with PhantomData<S> recording the state and impl blocks per state exposing only the legal transitions. Rust's ownership model supplies the half the class-based pattern lacks: transitions take self by value, so the old state is moved and cannot be reused, and the markers are erased, which makes the whole encoding free at run time. The separate-class-per-state form is still justified when the states carry different data, because one generic struct forces every state to share the same fields.
pitfalls: A transition that takes &self or &mut self cannot change the type: the value stays in its old state and the pattern silently stops working, so transitions must consume self.
Public fields or a public constructor let callers forge states; keep the marker field private and expose only the entry-point constructor.
Compile-fail tests (doctests with compile_fail, or a guard file excluded by a build tag) are required to prove the guarantee - a green test suite cannot show that an illegal transition is rejected.

PhantomData<S> participates in variance, drop check and auto-trait inference; switching to PhantomData<*const S> or PhantomData<fn() -> S> changes Send/Sync and drop semantics for reasons unrelated to the pattern.

variants.name: Proc-macro typestate DSL (trait per state)
variants.idiom_name: the typestate crate: #[automaton] + #[state] + a trait per state
variants.implementation_notes: The typestate crate generates the plumbing from a DSL: the annotated struct grows a state field, each state becomes a trait of the same name holding its legal transitions, and a generated sealed trait prevents new states from being added from outside. Choose it when the protocol is large enough that declaring states and transitions once is worth a macro dependency; the hand-written marker form stays more transparent and needs no procedural macros.
pitfalls: The macro hides the generated sealed trait and state field, so debugging type errors starts by expanding the macro.
The DSL supports unit-style states; states that need data must live inside the automaton or in a generated state enum, which changes the design.
